definition: Mawkish means characterized by sick sentimentality.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word mawkish. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know mawkish should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The gift-shop poems struck her as mawkish, all angel wings and rhyming sunsets with no real feeling underneath.
Sweet is far milder than mawkish — genuine tenderness that nobody could object to.
Syrupy is weaker than mawkish — heavily sweet, but not yet the false, sickening sentiment that makes an audience cringe.

Treacly is the British flavor of the fault: emotion thick and sticky as treacle, drowning a scene in sugar. It stops at excess, though — mawkish goes further, into sweetness so false it turns the stomach, the maggot still hiding in the word's history.

Saccharine means artificially sweet, like the sugar substitute it is named for — greeting-card sweetness a reader notices and distrusts. Mawkish is the harsher verdict: not just fake-sweet but sickening, emotion so false the audience recoils. A saccharine ad annoys; a mawkish one nauseates.

Middle English mawke, 'maggot,' survives nowhere else in the modern language, so mawkish has no living relatives to spot. What it kept instead is the feeling: when critics call an ending mawkish, they are literally saying it turned their stomach.
Mawkish means characterized by sick sentimentality.
The catalog copy for the memorial bench was mawkish overreach — 'where angels rest and grandpas watch forever' — and the carpenter refused to print it, saying the oak could speak for itself.
Mawkish is the harshest word on the sentimentality shelf: emotion so exaggerated and false that it sickens instead of moving.
The history is literal — the word began as 'maggoty,' sickening like spoiled meat — and the stomach-turn survives in its meaning.
Mawkish is the strongest insult in the sentimentality family: emotion so false and sugary it sickens — remember the maggot in its history.
Use sentimental for mild cases, and its unit-mate maudlin for tearful, self-indulgent people; save mawkish for art and rhetoric — the ad, the ending, the verse — that begs for tears it never earned.

When the committee met to choose a memorial for the town's flooded mill district, two designs made the final round.
The first was all sorrow on purpose: a weeping bronze child, an inscription in forced rhyme, and speakers hidden in the base to play the sound of soft rain.
Residents at the hearing called it mawkish.
One survivor said the grief on display felt manufactured, and that hearing fake rain where real water had taken homes made her feel sick.
The second design was a plain stone bench facing the river, carved with the names and one date.
Real sorrow, the committee wrote, does not need syrup poured over it.
